goals: State the laws of refraction and the conditions for a ray to pass undeviated
Say which of speed, wavelength and frequency change when light enters a denser medium
Calculate refractive index from speeds of light, and use v = f λ
Trace a ray through a glass block, mark the lateral displacement and explain multiple images in a thick mirror

slides.heading: Why does a straw look broken in a glass of nimbu pani?
slides.body_md: Part 1 — light changes direction when it crosses from one transparent medium into another. This bending is **refraction**.

rows: A straw looks broken at the surface of a drink
Light bends as it leaves the water
You see a faint reflection in a shop window
Part of the light is reflected at the glass
Writing under a glass paperweight looks raised
Light bends as it leaves the glass
A bathroom mirror shows a faint double image

visual.alt: Table of four everyday observations and the behaviour of light behind each

slides.narration: Namaste! Put a straw in a glass of nimbu pani and look from the side. The straw seems broken at the surface. Light is travelling from the drink into air and changing direction on the way. This bending of light at a boundary is called refraction. In this part we learn its laws and how to measure it.

slides.heading: Partial reflection and refraction
slides.body_md: When light meets the boundary between two transparent media, **part of it is reflected** back and **most of it is refracted** into the second medium. Going from a rarer medium (air) into a denser one (glass), the ray **bends towards the normal** ($r < i$); going from denser to rarer it **bends away from the normal**. The cause is the **change in the speed of light** from one medium to the other.

slides.narration: Here a ray in air strikes a flat glass surface. A small part of the light bounces back as a weak reflected ray. Most of it enters the glass and bends towards the normal, so the angle of refraction is smaller than the angle of incidence. Refraction happens because light travels at different speeds in different media.

slides.heading: The laws of refraction
slides.body_md:
**First law:** the incident ray, the refracted ray and the normal at the point of incidence all lie in **one plane**.

**Second law (Snell’s law):** for a given pair of media and a given colour of light, the ratio of the sine of the angle of incidence to the sine of the angle of refraction is a **constant**: $\dfrac{\sin i}{\sin r} = {}_{1}\mu_{2}$, the refractive index of medium 2 with respect to medium 1. In the graph, every reading for one glass lies on a straight line of slope 1.5.

visual.alt: Straight-line graph of sine of the angle of incidence against sine of the angle of refraction for glass, through the origin with slope one point five
visual.caption: Snell’s law: sin i is proportional to sin r.

slides.narration: Refraction obeys two laws. First, the incident ray, the refracted ray and the normal all lie in the same plane. Second, for a given pair of media and a given colour, the sine of the angle of incidence divided by the sine of the angle of refraction is always the same number. That constant is the refractive index.

slides.heading: Speed, wavelength and frequency

visual.alt: Table of what happens to speed, wavelength, frequency and colour when light enters glass from air

slides.narration: Light is a wave whose speed equals its frequency times its wavelength. When light enters water or glass from air, it slows down, and its wavelength becomes shorter in the same proportion. The frequency is set by the source and does not change, so the colour stays the same. A ray that meets the surface along the normal goes straight through.

slides.heading: Quick check: what stays the same?
slides.body_md: Decide which property of light is unchanged by refraction.
slides.narration: Quick check. Think about which property of light is fixed by the source.

slides.heading: Refractive index
slides.body_md:
The **absolute refractive index** of a medium is the ratio of the speed of light in vacuum (or air) to its speed in the medium:
$$\mu = \frac{c}{v}, \qquad c = 3 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$$
It is a pure number (**no unit**) and always **greater than 1** for a material medium. A **larger $\mu$** means light travels **more slowly** — the medium is **optically denser**. Refractive index depends on the **nature of the medium** and the **colour (wavelength)** of light, being slightly larger for violet than for red. Relative index: $\,{}_{1}\mu_{2} = \dfrac{\mu_{2}}{\mu_{1}} = \dfrac{v_{1}}{v_{2}}$.

visual.alt: Table of typical refractive indices and speeds of light in air, water, glass and diamond

slides.narration: The refractive index of a medium compares the speed of light in vacuum with its speed in the medium. It has no unit and is always more than one. Water has a refractive index of about one point three three, glass about one and a half, and diamond about two point four. The higher the index, the slower light travels in that medium.

slides.heading: Worked example: light in a sapphire
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Light of frequency $5.0 \times 10^{14}$ Hz passes from air into a sapphire of refractive index 1.76. Find (a) its speed in sapphire, (b) its wavelength in air, (c) its wavelength in sapphire.

**(a)** $v = \dfrac{c}{\mu} = \dfrac{3 \times 10^{8}}{1.76} = 1.70 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

**(b)** $\lambda_{air} = \dfrac{c}{f} = \dfrac{3 \times 10^{8}}{5.0 \times 10^{14}} = 6.0 \times 10^{-7}\ \text{m} = 600\ \text{nm}$.

**(c)** $\lambda = \dfrac{v}{f} = \dfrac{\lambda_{air}}{\mu} = \dfrac{600}{1.76} \approx 341\ \text{nm}$. The frequency is unchanged.

visual.alt: Table of speed, frequency and wavelength of the light in air and in sapphire

slides.narration: Divide the speed of light in air by the refractive index to get its speed in sapphire, about one point seven times ten to the eight metres per second. The wavelength in air is speed divided by frequency, six hundred nanometres. Inside the sapphire the frequency stays the same, so the wavelength shrinks by the same factor as the speed, to about three hundred and forty nanometres.

slides.body_md: Find a refractive index from the speed of light in a medium.
slides.narration: Quick check. Refractive index is the speed in air divided by the speed in the medium.

slides.heading: Refraction through a rectangular glass block
slides.body_md: A ray entering a glass block bends **towards the normal** at the first face and **away from the normal** at the second. Because the two faces are **parallel**, the angle of emergence equals the angle of incidence ($e = i$), so the **emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray** but **shifted sideways**. The perpendicular distance between the incident ray produced and the emergent ray is the **lateral displacement**. It increases with (1) the **thickness** of the block, (2) the **angle of incidence**, (3) the **refractive index** of the glass; and it is zero for normal incidence.

slides.narration: Follow the ray through the block. At the top face it bends towards the normal. At the bottom face it bends away by exactly the same amount, because the faces are parallel. So the ray comes out parallel to its original direction, but shifted sideways. This sideways shift is the lateral displacement. A thicker block, a larger angle of incidence or a denser glass makes it larger.

slides.heading: Worked example: angles in a glass block
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A ray strikes the top face of a glass block ($\mu = 1.5$) at $i = 50^\circ$. Find (a) the angle of refraction and (b) the angle of emergence at the bottom face.

**(a)** $\sin r = \dfrac{\sin 50^\circ}{1.5} = \dfrac{0.766}{1.5} = 0.511$, so $r \approx 30.7^\circ$.

**(b)** At the bottom face the ray meets the glass–air surface at $30.7^\circ$: $\sin e = 1.5 \times \sin 30.7^\circ = 1.5 \times 0.511 = 0.766$, so $e = 50^\circ = i$. The emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray.

visual.alt: Table of the angles at the two faces of the glass block

slides.narration: Use Snell’s law at the first face. The sine of fifty degrees is about point seven six six; divide by one and a half to get about point five one, which is the sine of roughly thirty one degrees. At the second face, run the law the other way. The ray comes out at fifty degrees again, so it is parallel to the incident ray.

slides.narration: Quick check. Remember that the two faces of the block are parallel.

slides.heading: Multiple images in a thick plane mirror
slides.body_md: An ordinary mirror is a sheet of glass **silvered at the back**. Light from an object is (1) **partly reflected at the front glass surface**, giving a **faint** image; (2) mostly **refracted into the glass, reflected by the silvered back** and refracted out — the **brightest** image (the second one); (3) partly reflected **again and again** inside the glass, giving more images that get **fainter**. All the emerging rays are **parallel**, so the eye sees a row of images. A candle flame viewed obliquely in a thick mirror shows this well.

slides.narration: A household mirror is thick glass with a silver coating at the back. A little light reflects from the front glass surface and gives a faint first image. Most of the light goes into the glass, reflects off the silver and comes back out, giving the brightest image. Some light keeps bouncing inside the glass, giving more images that grow fainter and fainter.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 1
bullets: Refraction: change in direction of light at a boundary, caused by a change in speed; partial reflection also occurs.
Laws: one plane; sin i / sin r = constant (Snell’s law).
Into a denser medium: speed and wavelength decrease, frequency and colour unchanged.
μ = c / v, no unit, greater than 1; undeviated ray when i = 0 or the media have equal μ.
Glass block: e = i, emergent ray parallel, lateral displacement grows with thickness, i and μ.
Thick mirror: several images; the second (from the silvered back) is the brightest.

rows: Emergent ray parallel to incident ray

visual.alt: Summary table of four key relations from Part 1

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part 1. Light bends at a boundary because its speed changes. The two laws of refraction tell us the rays lie in one plane and the ratio of sines is constant. Entering a denser medium, light slows down and its wavelength shrinks, but its frequency stays fixed. A glass block shifts a ray sideways without changing its direction.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 1
bullets: Measure i and r from the normal, never from the surface.
Say “frequency does not change” when asked what happens to light entering water.
Refractive index has no unit; never write one.
In a glass-block diagram, draw the emergent ray parallel to the incident ray and mark the lateral displacement as a perpendicular distance.

rows: Speed and wavelength decrease; frequency is unchanged
μ = c / v, always more than 1
Draw it perpendicular to both rays

visual.alt: Table of four common slips in Part 1 and their fixes

slides.narration: Some tips for the exam. Always measure angles from the normal. When light enters a denser medium, its speed and wavelength fall but its frequency stays the same. Refractive index is a ratio of speeds, so it has no unit and is more than one. In a glass block diagram, show the emergent ray parallel to the incident ray.

slides.heading: Things are not where they seem
slides.body_md: Part 2 — refraction makes water look shallow, lets a prism bend light towards its base, and, past a certain angle, stops light leaving glass at all.

rows: A pond looks shallower than it is
A prism bends a beam towards its base
A periscope uses prisms, not mirrors

slides.narration: In this part we see more effects of refraction. A pond looks shallower than it really is, which can be dangerous for swimmers. A glass prism bends light towards its thick base. And if light inside glass meets the surface at a large enough angle, none of it escapes; it is all reflected back. We will see how periscopes use this.

slides.heading: Real and apparent depth
slides.body_md:
Rays from a coin at the bottom of a pool bend **away from the normal** as they leave the water. Produced backwards, they meet at a point **above** the coin, so the coin appears **raised**: the pool looks **shallower**. For viewing from directly above,
$$\mu = \frac{\text{real depth}}{\text{apparent depth}}$$
The **shift** (apparent rise) $= \text{real depth} - \text{apparent depth} = \text{real depth}\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{\mu}\right)$. Viewed **obliquely**, the object appears raised even more.

slides.narration: Rays from a coin at the bottom of a pool bend away from the normal as they come out into air. Your eye traces them back in straight lines, to a point above the coin. So the coin seems raised and the pool looks shallower. For viewing straight down, the refractive index equals the real depth divided by the apparent depth.

slides.heading: Worked example: a fish tank
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A small pebble lies at the bottom of a fish tank filled with water ($\mu = \frac{4}{3}$) to a depth of 36 cm. (a) How deep does the pebble appear when viewed from directly above? (b) By how much does it appear raised?

**(a)** $\text{apparent depth} = \dfrac{\text{real depth}}{\mu} = \dfrac{36}{4/3} = \dfrac{36 \times 3}{4} = 27\ \text{cm}$.

**(b)** $\text{shift} = 36 - 27 = 9\ \text{cm}$.

visual.alt: Table of the values in the fish tank example

slides.narration: The apparent depth is the real depth divided by the refractive index. Thirty six divided by four thirds is thirty six times three quarters, which is twenty seven centimetres. So the pebble seems to sit twenty seven centimetres down, and it looks raised by nine centimetres. That is a quarter of the real depth.

slides.heading: Effects of apparent depth
slides.body_md:
The same refraction explains several everyday effects:
- A **stick or ruler** dipped obliquely in water appears **bent at the surface**, the immersed part looking **raised** and shorter.
- A **pond or pool** looks shallower than it is — a real danger for swimmers.
- Letters under a **glass slab** appear raised; the rise for a slab of thickness $t$ is $t\left(1 - \frac{1}{\mu}\right)$.
- A **fish** in water appears nearer the surface; to the fish, a bird above appears **higher** than it is.

Each point of the immersed part appears raised

Bird looks higher to a fish
Light bends towards the normal entering water

visual.alt: Table of four effects of refraction at a plane surface and their reasons

slides.narration: Apparent depth explains many things. A stick dipped slantwise into water seems bent at the surface, because every point under water looks raised. A pool looks shallower than it is, so never judge its depth by eye. Print under a glass block seems lifted. And to a fish looking up, a bird in the air appears higher than it really is.

slides.heading: Refraction through a triangular prism
slides.body_md: A prism has two **refracting faces** inclined at the **angle of the prism**, $A$. A ray bends **towards the normal** at the first face and **away from the normal** at the second, so it is turned **towards the base**. The angle between the incident ray produced and the emergent ray is the **angle of deviation** $\delta$. Inside the prism $r_{1} + r_{2} = A$, and $\delta = i + e - A$. Deviation depends on the angle of incidence, the angle of the prism, the material and the colour of light; as $i$ is increased, $\delta$ first **decreases** to a **minimum** and then **increases**.

slides.narration: In a prism the two faces are not parallel, so the bending at the second face does not undo the bending at the first. Both bends turn the ray towards the thick base. The angle between the original direction and the final direction is the angle of deviation. It depends on the angle of incidence, the prism angle, the glass and the colour of the light.

slides.heading: Worked example: deviation by a prism
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A ray falls on one face of a glass prism ($\mu = 1.5$) of angle $A = 60^\circ$ at $i = 40^\circ$. The angle of refraction at the first face is $r_{1} = 25.4^\circ$ and the ray emerges at $e = 58.5^\circ$. Find (a) $r_{2}$, the angle of incidence inside at the second face, and (b) the angle of deviation.

**(a)** $r_{1} + r_{2} = A$, so $r_{2} = 60 - 25.4 = 34.6$, that is $34.6^\circ$.

**(b)** $\delta = i + e - A = 40 + 58.5 - 60 = 38.5$, that is $38.5^\circ$, towards the base.

visual.alt: Flow from the incident ray through the angles inside the prism to the emergent ray and the deviation

slides.narration: Inside the prism, the two angles of refraction add up to the prism angle, so the second one is sixty minus twenty five point four, or thirty four point six degrees. The deviation is the angle of incidence plus the angle of emergence minus the prism angle: forty plus fifty eight and a half minus sixty, which gives thirty eight and a half degrees, towards the base.

slides.heading: Critical angle and total internal reflection
slides.body_md:
When light goes from a **denser to a rarer** medium, it bends away from the normal. As $i$ increases, $r$ reaches $90^\circ$; that angle of incidence in the denser medium is the **critical angle** $C$. For a medium in air,
$$\mu = \frac{1}{\sin C}$$
If $i > C$, no light is refracted: **all** of it is reflected back — **total internal reflection (TIR)**. **Conditions:** (1) light must travel from a **denser to a rarer** medium; (2) the angle of incidence must be **greater than the critical angle**. Critical angles: glass about $42^\circ$, water about $49^\circ$, diamond about $24^\circ$.

At one special angle, the critical angle, the escaping ray just skims along the surface. Beyond that angle, no light escapes at all. It is all reflected back inside. This is total internal reflection, and it happens only when light goes from a denser to a rarer medium.

slides.heading: Worked example: critical angle of glass
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Find the critical angle for a glass–air surface if the refractive index of the glass is 1.5. Will a ray inside the glass meeting the surface at $45^\circ$ escape?

**Step 1.** $\sin C = \dfrac{1}{\mu} = \dfrac{1}{1.5} = 0.667$.

**Step 2.** From tables, $\sin 41.8^\circ = 0.667$, so $C \approx 41.8^\circ$.

**Step 3.** $45^\circ > 41.8^\circ$ and light is going from glass to air, so the ray is **totally internally reflected** — it does not escape.

slides.narration: The sine of the critical angle is one divided by the refractive index. For glass of index one and a half, that is about point six six seven, which is the sine of nearly forty two degrees. A ray inside the glass at forty five degrees is past the critical angle, so it cannot get out; it is totally reflected.

slides.body_md: Decide whether light inside glass escapes or is totally reflected.

slides.heading: Totally reflecting prisms
slides.body_md:
A right-angled **isosceles** glass prism (angles $45^\circ$, $45^\circ$, $90^\circ$) makes an excellent reflector because rays meet the faces inside at $45^\circ$, which is **more than the critical angle** of glass ($42^\circ$).
- Light entering a **short face normally** is totally reflected at the hypotenuse face and **turned through 90°** — used in **periscopes**.
- Light entering the **hypotenuse face normally** is totally reflected at both short faces and **turned through 180°** — used in **binoculars** and in cycle **reflectors**.
- In an **equilateral prism** (60°) a ray inside can also meet a face beyond the critical angle and be totally reflected.

slides.narration: A glass prism with angles of forty five, forty five and ninety degrees makes a perfect mirror. Light inside it meets a face at forty five degrees, which is more than the critical angle of glass. Sending light in through a short face turns it through a right angle, as in a periscope. Sending it in through the long face turns it right round, as in binoculars.

slides.heading: Prism reflector or plane mirror?
slides.body_md:
Total internal reflection in a prism is better than reflection from a silvered plane mirror because:
1. **All** the light is reflected (100%), so the image is **brighter**; a mirror absorbs some light.
2. There is **only one image** — no multiple images from a thick mirror.
3. There is **no silvering** to tarnish or peel off with time.

Other uses of TIR: the **sparkle of a diamond** (small critical angle, so light is trapped and reflected many times) and **optical fibres**.

slides.narration: Why do good periscopes and binoculars use prisms instead of mirrors? A prism reflects all the light by total internal reflection, so images are brighter. notes.title: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Refraction and its laws
sections.body_md:
- **Refraction:** the change in direction of light as it passes obliquely from one transparent medium into another. **Cause:** light has different speeds in different media.
- At every boundary there is also **partial reflection** (a faint reflection in a window pane).
- Rarer → denser: ray bends **towards** the normal; denser → rarer: **away** from the normal.
- **Laws of refraction:** (1) incident ray, refracted ray and normal at the point of incidence lie in one plane; (2) **Snell’s law** — $\sin i / \sin r$ is constant for a given pair of media and a given colour.
- On entering a denser medium: **speed and wavelength decrease**, **frequency (and so colour) is unchanged**.
- **No deviation** when (i) $i = 0$ (along the normal) or (ii) both media have the same refractive index.

key_terms.definition_md: Bending of light when it passes obliquely from one transparent medium into another, because its speed changes.
For a given pair of media and colour of light, the sine of the angle of incidence divided by the sine of the angle of refraction is a constant.

visual.alt: Table of the changes in light on entering a denser medium

sections.heading: 2. Refractive index
sections.body_md:
- **Absolute refractive index:** $\mu = c / v$, with $c = 3 \times 10^{8}$ m s⁻¹. No unit; greater than 1 for every material medium.
- Larger $\mu$ → slower light → **optically denser** (optical density is not the same as mass density: kerosene is optically denser than water but floats on it).
- **Relative refractive index:** $\,{}_{1}\mu_{2} = \mu_{2} / \mu_{1} = v_{1} / v_{2}$.
- $\mu$ depends on the **material**, the **colour (wavelength)** of light (larger for violet than red) and slightly on **temperature**.
- Typical values: water 1.33, glass 1.5, diamond 2.42.

key_terms.definition_md: Ratio of the speed of light in vacuum to the speed of light in the medium.
A medium with a larger refractive index, in which light travels more slowly.

visual.alt: Table of refractive indices and speeds of light in three media

sections.heading: 3. Rectangular glass block and thick mirror
sections.body_md:
- Ray bends towards the normal at the first face and away at the second; the faces are parallel, so **e = i** and the **emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray**.
- **Lateral displacement:** perpendicular distance between the incident ray produced and the emergent ray. It increases with the **thickness** of the block, the **angle of incidence** and the **refractive index**; it is zero for normal incidence.
- **Thick plane mirror (silvered at the back):** partial reflection at the front glass surface gives a faint first image; reflection at the silvered back gives the **brightest (second)** image; repeated internal reflections give further, fainter images. All emergent rays are parallel.

key_terms.definition_md: The perpendicular distance between the incident ray produced and the emergent ray of a parallel-sided block.
The angle between the emergent ray and the normal at the second face.

rows: Reflection at the front glass surface

visual.alt: Table of the images formed by a thick plane mirror

sections.heading: 4. Real and apparent depth
sections.body_md:
- Rays from an object under water bend away from the normal on leaving; produced back they meet **above** the object, which appears **raised**.
- For near-normal viewing: $\mu = \dfrac{\text{real depth}}{\text{apparent depth}}$.
- **Shift (apparent rise)** $= \text{real depth} - \text{apparent depth} = \text{real depth}\,(1 - 1/\mu)$.
- Viewed obliquely, the object appears raised even more.
- Effects: a pool looks shallower; a stick dipped obliquely looks bent at the surface; print under a glass block looks raised; to a fish, a bird looks higher.

key_terms.definition_md: The depth at which an object in a denser medium appears to be when viewed from the rarer medium.
The distance by which an object under a denser medium appears raised: real depth minus apparent depth.

formulas.label: Apparent rise for real depth d

visual.alt: Table of real depth, refractive index, apparent depth and shift for three cases

sections.heading: 5. Refraction through a triangular prism
sections.body_md:
- A prism has two refracting faces inclined at the **angle of the prism** $A$.
- The ray bends towards the normal at the first face and away from it at the second; the emergent ray is turned **towards the base**.
- **Angle of deviation** $\delta$: angle between the incident ray produced and the emergent ray.
- Relations: $r_{1} + r_{2} = A$; $\delta = i + e - A$.
- $\delta$ depends on (i) angle of incidence, (ii) angle of the prism, (iii) refractive index of the material, (iv) colour of light (violet deviates most). As $i$ increases, $\delta$ first decreases to a minimum, then increases.

key_terms.definition_md: The angle between the direction of the incident ray and the direction of the emergent ray.
The angle between the two refracting faces of a prism.

visual.alt: Table of factors that change the angle of deviation of a prism

sections.heading: 6. Critical angle and total internal reflection
sections.body_md:
- **Critical angle C:** the angle of incidence in the denser medium for which the angle of refraction in the rarer medium is $90^\circ$.
- For a medium in air: $\mu = 1 / \sin C$.
- **Total internal reflection (TIR):** when $i > C$, all the light is reflected back into the denser medium. **Conditions:** light travels from denser to rarer; $i > C$.
- **Totally reflecting prisms** (45°–45°–90° glass, $C \approx 42^\circ$): enter a short face normally → turned through 90° (periscope); enter the hypotenuse face normally → turned through 180° (binoculars, reflectors). An equilateral prism can also reflect totally at a face.
- Advantages over a plane mirror: all light reflected (brighter), one image only, no silvering to spoil.

key_terms.definition_md: The angle of incidence in the denser medium for which the refracted ray grazes the surface (angle of refraction 90°).
Reflection of all the light back into a denser medium when it meets the boundary with a rarer medium at more than the critical angle.

visual.alt: Table of critical angles of water, glass and diamond

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Measuring angles from the surface instead of the normal.
- Saying the frequency of light changes in glass.
- Writing apparent depth = real depth × μ.
- Giving only one condition for total internal reflection.
- Drawing the emergent ray of a glass block not parallel to the incident ray.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- Calculations: formula, substitution, answer (and unit where there is one; μ has none).
- Ray diagrams: arrows on rays, normals drawn dotted, angles labelled, emergent ray direction correct.
- TIR: both conditions, each with its key word (denser to rarer; greater than the critical angle).

questions.stem_md: Orange light from a sodium street lamp passes from air into the glass of a car windscreen. Which property of the light does NOT change?

options.text_md: Its frequency
Its speed
Its wavelength
Its direction, for a ray falling obliquely

questions.solution_md: Frequency is fixed by the source; speed and wavelength both fall in glass, and an oblique ray bends — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A laser beam strikes the flat glass wall of an aquarium along the normal. Inside the glass the beam:

options.text_md: bends towards the normal
bends away from the normal
goes straight on, but travels more slowly
is totally reflected back

questions.solution_md: For i = 0 there is no change of direction, only a change of speed — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Standing outside a sweet shop at night, Rehan sees the sweets through the window and also a faint reflection of himself in the same glass. This shows that at a glass surface:

options.text_md: all the light is refracted
part of the light is reflected and the rest is refracted
all the light is reflected
light is absorbed and then given out again

questions.solution_md: Partial reflection and refraction happen together at a boundary — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A glass rod of refractive index 1.47 almost disappears when it is dipped in a beaker of glycerine. The refractive index of glycerine is most likely:

options.text_md: about 1.47, the same as that of the rod
about 1.00
about 2.42
about 0.68, the reciprocal of 1.47

questions.solution_md: Light passes undeviated, with no reflection, between media of equal refractive index, so the boundary cannot be seen — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A ray of light going obliquely from water into air bends away from the normal.

**Reason (R):** Light travels faster in air than in water.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true; the increase in speed is the cause of bending away — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A beam of light that falls along the normal on a glass block passes through it without changing direction.

**Reason (R):** The frequency of light does not change when it enters glass.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both statements are true, but the undeviated path is due to i = 0, not to the constant frequency — option (b).

questions.stem_md: True or false? When light passes from air into water, its wavelength becomes shorter but its frequency stays the same.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True: v = fλ with f fixed, so λ falls with v.

questions.stem_md: The incident ray, the refracted ray and the normal at the point of incidence all lie in the same ___.
questions.solution_md: **Plane** (first law of refraction).

questions.stem_md: Why does a beam of torchlight change direction when it passes slantwise from air into a pond?

answer.model_answer_md: Because the speed of light in water is less than in air.

questions.solution_md: Change of speed.

questions.stem_md: Ishaan says, “A ray of light always bends when it passes from one transparent medium into another.” State two situations that prove him wrong.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) When the ray falls along the normal to the boundary (angle of incidence zero). (ii) When the two media have the same refractive index, so the speed of light does not change, for example a glass rod in a liquid of equal refractive index.

questions.solution_md: Normal incidence; equal refractive indices.

questions.stem_md: Riya sends a ray from air into a block of clear perspex at several angles of incidence. For each reading, sin i ÷ sin r comes to about 1.49, and the rays always stay on the drawing paper. State the two laws of refraction that her results illustrate.

answer.model_answer_md: (1) The incident ray, the refracted ray and the normal at the point of incidence lie in one plane. (2) For a given pair of media and a given colour of light, sin i ÷ sin r is constant (Snell’s law); here the constant, about 1.49, is the refractive index of perspex.

questions.solution_md: Two laws.

questions.stem_md: A ray of light in air meets the surface of a clear liquid at an angle of incidence of 45°. The angle of refraction is 30°. Calculate the refractive index of the liquid, to three significant figures. (sin 45° = 0.7071, sin 30° = 0.5)
Light travels at 2.0 × 10⁸ m/s in a sheet of acrylic. Taking the speed of light in air as 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s, the refractive index of the acrylic is:
questions.solution_md: $\mu = \dfrac{c}{v} = \dfrac{3.0 \times 10^{8}}{2.0 \times 10^{8}} = 1.5$ — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A ray passes obliquely from turpentine (refractive index 1.47) into a ruby (refractive index 1.76). In the ruby, the ray:

options.text_md: speeds up and bends away from the normal
slows down and bends away from the normal
keeps the same speed and direction
slows down and bends towards the normal

questions.solution_md: Ruby has the larger refractive index, so it is optically denser: light slows and bends towards the normal — option (d).

questions.stem_md: The orange-yellow glow of a lamp has a wavelength of 600 nm in air. Inside a glass slab with μ = 1.5, its wavelength becomes:

options.text_md: 900 nm
600 nm
400 nm
300 nm

questions.solution_md: Frequency is unchanged, so $\lambda_{glass} = \dfrac{\lambda_{air}}{\mu} = \dfrac{600}{1.5} = 400$ nm — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Kerosene (refractive index 1.44) floats on water (refractive index 1.33). Which statement is correct?

options.text_md: Water is optically denser because it is heavier
Kerosene is optically denser than water even though its mass density is lower
Both are equally dense optically
Light travels faster in kerosene than in water

questions.solution_md: Optical density depends on refractive index, not on mass density — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A flash of light crosses a glass window pane 3.0 cm thick, along the normal. The refractive index of the glass is 1.5. How long does the light take to cross the pane? Give your answer in units of 10⁻¹⁰ s.
In a sample of mustard oil, light travels at 2.04 × 10⁸ m/s. Find the refractive index of the oil, to three significant figures. (c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s)
A red laser emits light of wavelength 7.5 × 10⁻⁷ m in air. Find its frequency in units of 10¹⁴ Hz. (c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s)
questions.solution_md: $f = \dfrac{c}{\lambda} = \dfrac{3.0 \times 10^{8}}{7.5 \times 10^{-7}} = 4.0 \times 10^{14}$ Hz, so in units of $10^{14}$ Hz the frequency is $\dfrac{4.0 \times 10^{14}}{10^{14}} = 4$.

questions.stem_md: The speed of light is 2.25 × 10⁸ m/s in the water of an aquarium and 2.0 × 10⁸ m/s in its glass wall. Find the refractive index of the glass with respect to the water, to three significant figures.
Refractive index has no ___ because it is the ratio of two speeds.
questions.solution_md: **Unit**.

questions.stem_md: True or false? The absolute refractive index of a transparent solid can be less than 1.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False: light is slower in any material than in vacuum, so c/v is greater than 1.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A green traffic light seen by a diver under water still looks green.

**Reason (R):** The frequency of light, which decides its colour, does not change on refraction.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and R explains A — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Write the relation between the refractive index μ of a medium, the speed of light c in vacuum and its speed v in the medium.

answer.model_answer_md: μ = c ÷ v (the ratio of the speed in vacuum to the speed in the medium).

questions.solution_md: μ = c/v.

questions.stem_md: Light travels at 1.24 × 10⁸ m/s in diamond and at 2.0 × 10⁸ m/s in crown glass. (a) Calculate the refractive index of diamond. (b) Which of the two is optically denser? Give a reason.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) $\mu = \dfrac{3.0 \times 10^{8}}{1.24 \times 10^{8}} \approx 2.42$. (b) Diamond, because light travels more slowly in it (its refractive index, about 2.42, is larger than that of glass, 1.5).

questions.solution_md: About 2.42; diamond.

questions.stem_md: A green laser has a frequency of 5.6 × 10¹⁴ Hz. Its beam passes from air into water of refractive index 4/3. Calculate (a) the wavelength in air, (b) the speed of light in water, (c) the wavelength in water, each to three significant figures. (c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s)

answer.model_answer_md: (a) $\lambda = \dfrac{c}{f} = \dfrac{3.0 \times 10^{8}}{5.6 \times 10^{14}} \approx 5.36 \times 10^{-7}$ m (536 nm). (b) $v = \dfrac{c}{\mu} = 3.0 \times 10^{8} \times \dfrac{3}{4} = 2.25 \times 10^{8}$ m/s. (c) $\lambda_{w} = \dfrac{v}{f} = \dfrac{2.25 \times 10^{8}}{5.6 \times 10^{14}} \approx 4.02 \times 10^{-7}$ m (402 nm); the frequency is unchanged.

questions.stem_md: A ray strikes one face of a parallel-sided glass block at an angle of incidence of 40°. Inside the glass it travels at about 25° to the normal. The ray leaving the opposite face makes with the normal an angle of:
questions.solution_md: The faces are parallel, so the ray meets the second face at 25° and leaves at the original angle, 40° — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Which change makes the lateral displacement of a ray passing through a glass block larger?

options.text_md: Using a thicker block of the same glass, at the same angle of incidence
Making the angle of incidence zero
Using a block of glass of lower refractive index
Moving the light source farther away along the same ray

questions.solution_md: Lateral displacement grows with thickness, angle of incidence and refractive index; it is zero at normal incidence — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A candle flame is viewed obliquely in a thick plane mirror silvered at the back, and a row of images is seen. The brightest image is formed by:

options.text_md: reflection at the silvered back surface
reflection at the front glass surface
the last of the repeated reflections inside the glass
none — all the images are equally bright

questions.solution_md: Most of the light enters the glass and is reflected strongly by the silvering, giving the second (brightest) image — option (a).

questions.stem_md: True or false? A ray that falls normally on a rectangular glass block has zero lateral displacement.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True: it passes straight through without any sideways shift.

questions.stem_md: The perpendicular distance between the incident ray produced and the emergent ray of a glass block is called the lateral ___.
questions.solution_md: **Displacement** (lateral shift).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A thick plane mirror silvered at the back forms several images of a bright object.

**Reason (R):** Light undergoes repeated partial reflection and refraction between the front glass surface and the silvered back.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and R explains A — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Sana traces a ray through a glass block of refractive index 1.5 with an angle of incidence of 50° and measures the angle of refraction as 31°. (a) What angle does the emergent ray make with the normal at the far face? (b) Name the three factors on which the lateral displacement depends.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) 50°, equal to the angle of incidence, because the two faces of the block are parallel. (b) The thickness of the block, the angle of incidence and the refractive index of the glass.

questions.solution_md: 50°; thickness, i, μ.

questions.stem_md: Ananya looks obliquely at a lamp in a thick bathroom mirror and sees a faint image, then a bright image, then fainter ones. Explain how the first two images are formed.

answer.model_answer_md: The first, faint image comes from the small fraction of light reflected straight off the front glass surface. The second, brightest image comes from the light that enters the glass, is reflected by the silvered back and refracts out again; most of the light follows this path.

questions.solution_md: Front surface; silvered back.

questions.stem_md: A ring dropped into a beaker of kerosene (refractive index 1.44) lies 7.2 cm below the surface. Seen from directly above, it appears to be at a depth of:

options.text_md: 2.2 cm
7.2 cm
5 cm

questions.solution_md: $\text{apparent depth} = \dfrac{7.2}{1.44} = 5$ cm — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A glass paperweight 6.0 cm thick (refractive index 1.5) rests on a printed page. By how many centimetres does the print appear to be raised when viewed from directly above?
questions.solution_md: Apparent depth $= \dfrac{6.0}{1.5} = 4.0$ cm; shift $= 6.0 - 4.0 = 2.0$ cm.

questions.stem_md: A water tank looks 0.9 m deep when seen from directly above. Taking the refractive index of water as 4/3, find its real depth in metres.
questions.solution_md: Real depth $= \mu \times \text{apparent depth} = \dfrac{4}{3} \times 0.9 = 1.2$ m.

questions.stem_md: A travelling microscope is focused on a cross mark. A glass block 4.5 cm thick is placed over the mark, and the microscope must be raised by 1.5 cm to focus on the mark again. Find the refractive index of the glass.
questions.solution_md: Apparent depth $= 4.5 - 1.5 = 3.0$ cm; $\mu = \dfrac{\text{real depth}}{\text{apparent depth}} = \dfrac{4.5}{3.0} = 1.5$.

questions.stem_md: Kabir holds a straight steel ruler slantwise in a bucket of water. Looking from above, he sees that the part of the ruler under water:

options.text_md: appears lowered, so the ruler looks bent downwards
looks exactly in line with the part in air
cannot be seen at all
appears raised, so the ruler looks bent upwards at the water surface

questions.solution_md: Every point under water appears raised, so the immersed part looks lifted and the ruler looks bent at the surface — option (d).

questions.stem_md: True or false? A coin at the bottom of a bucket of water, seen from directly above, appears deeper than it really is.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False: it appears raised; apparent depth = real depth ÷ μ is less than the real depth.

questions.stem_md: Refractive index of water = real depth ÷ ___ depth.
questions.solution_md: **Apparent**.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A fish in a pond appears to a boy on the bank to be nearer the surface than it actually is.

**Reason (R):** Light from the fish bends towards the normal as it comes out of the water into air.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true; R is false — light leaving water bends away from the normal — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A coin in a pool is first viewed from directly above and then from a slant. In which case does it appear nearer the surface?

answer.model_answer_md: When viewed from a slant (obliquely): the apparent rise is larger.

questions.solution_md: Oblique viewing.

questions.stem_md: A lifeguard warns children that a swimming pool is deeper than it looks. Explain, in terms of refraction, why the pool looks shallower than it is.

answer.model_answer_md: Light from the floor of the pool bends away from the normal as it passes from water into air. The eye follows the emergent rays back in straight lines, and they appear to come from a point above the floor. So the floor appears raised and the pool looks shallower.

questions.solution_md: Bending away from normal; image raised.

marking_scheme.step: Bending away from the normal at the surface
Rays traced back meet above the floor

questions.stem_md: A glass beaker contains water (refractive index 4/3) to a depth of 16 cm, with a small bead at the bottom. (a) Find the apparent depth of the bead. (b) By how much does the bead appear raised? (c) The water is replaced by a liquid of refractive index 1.6 to the same depth. What is the new apparent depth?

answer.model_answer_md: (a) $\dfrac{16}{4/3} = 12$ cm. (b) $16 - 12 = 4$ cm. (c) $\dfrac{16}{1.6} = 10$ cm — the denser liquid makes the bead look even nearer.

questions.solution_md: 12 cm; 4 cm; 10 cm.

questions.stem_md: A narrow beam of red laser light passes through a glass prism standing on its base. Compared with the incident beam, the emergent beam is:

options.text_md: turned towards the apex of the prism
turned towards the base of the prism
parallel to the incident beam but shifted
reflected back towards the laser

questions.solution_md: Refraction at both inclined faces turns the ray towards the base — option (b).

questions.stem_md: In a prism experiment with a prism of angle 60°, Tanvi measures the angle of incidence as 55° and the angle of emergence as 46°. Find the angle of deviation, in degrees.
questions.solution_md: $\delta = i + e - A = 55 + 46 - 60 = 41$, so the deviation is $41^\circ$.

questions.stem_md: A ray enters an equilateral glass prism (angle 60°). The angle of refraction at the first face is 28°. Find the angle at which the ray meets the second face inside the prism, in degrees.
The angle of deviation produced by a glass prism does NOT depend on:

options.text_md: the angle of incidence
the refractive index of the glass
how far the light source is from the prism
the angle of the prism

questions.solution_md: Deviation depends on i, A, the material and the colour of light, not on the distance of the source — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? As the angle of incidence on a prism is slowly increased from a small value, the angle of deviation first decreases and then increases.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True: deviation passes through a minimum value.

questions.stem_md: The angle between the incident ray produced and the emergent ray of a prism is called the angle of ___.
questions.solution_md: **Deviation**.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** When light passes from the glass of a prism back into air, its speed decreases.

**Reason (R):** Glass is optically denser than air.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is false — light speeds up on entering air; R is true — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Rohan says the deviation produced by his prism “depends only on the angle of the prism”. Name four factors on which it actually depends.

answer.model_answer_md: The angle of incidence, the angle of the prism, the refractive index of the material of the prism, and the colour (wavelength) of the light used.

questions.solution_md: i, A, μ, colour.

questions.stem_md: The critical angle for a certain glass–air surface is 42°. A ray inside the glass meets this surface at an angle of incidence of 50°. The ray:

options.text_md: passes into air, bending away from the normal
passes into air without bending
grazes along the surface
is totally reflected back into the glass

questions.solution_md: Glass to air and 50° > 42°, so total internal reflection occurs — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Calculate the critical angle for light going from water (refractive index 4/3) into air, correct to one decimal place, in degrees.
A plastic used to make a decorative light pipe has a critical angle of 40° with air. Find its refractive index, to three significant figures. (sin 40° = 0.643)
Total internal reflection can take place when light travels:

options.text_md: from air towards glass, at any angle of incidence
from glass towards air, at an angle smaller than the critical angle
from glass towards air, at an angle of incidence greater than the critical angle
from air towards water, at an angle greater than the critical angle

questions.solution_md: Both conditions: denser to rarer, and i greater than C — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Light enters one of the shorter faces of a right-angled isosceles glass prism along the normal. After total internal reflection at the hypotenuse face, it is turned through:
questions.solution_md: It meets the hypotenuse at 45° (> 42°), is totally reflected and leaves the other short face at right angles to its original direction — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A cycle reflector contains tiny right-angled isosceles prisms. Light enters through the hypotenuse face along the normal. It comes out:

options.text_md: turned through 90°
without any change in direction
spread out into colours, turned through 45°
travelling back in the direction it came from, turned through 180°

questions.solution_md: Two total internal reflections, each at 45°, reverse the ray — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Diamond (refractive index 2.42) sparkles far more than glass (refractive index 1.5) cut in the same shape, because diamond has:

options.text_md: a much smaller critical angle (about 24°), so light is trapped and totally reflected many times inside it
a larger critical angle, so more light escapes at once
a silvered back surface
a lower refractive index, so light travels faster in it

questions.solution_md: $\sin C = \dfrac{1}{2.42} = 0.413$, so $C \approx 24^\circ$, much smaller than about $42^\circ$ for glass — option (a).

questions.stem_md: True or false? A totally reflecting prism reflects practically all the light falling on it, while a silvered plane mirror absorbs a small part of it.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True: this is one advantage of the prism.

questions.stem_md: The angle of incidence in the denser medium for which the angle of refraction in the rarer medium is 90° is called the ___ angle.
questions.solution_md: **Critical**.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Total internal reflection cannot occur when light passes from air into water.

**Reason (R):** A ray entering an optically denser medium bends towards the normal, so the angle of refraction never reaches 90°.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and R explains A — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Name the phenomenon that lets a 45°–45°–90° glass prism act as a perfect reflector in a periscope.

answer.model_answer_md: Total internal reflection.

questions.solution_md: TIR.

questions.stem_md: A periscope for a school model submarine can be built with two plane mirrors or two right-angled isosceles prisms. Give two reasons why the prisms are the better choice.

answer.model_answer_md: Prisms reflect all the incident light by total internal reflection, so the image is brighter; a thick mirror also gives faint extra images, while a prism gives only one. A prism has no silver coating, so it does not tarnish or peel with age.

questions.solution_md: Brighter, single image, no silvering.

questions.stem_md: Inside a glass block (refractive index 1.5), rays meet the glass–air surface at angles of incidence of (a) 30°, (b) 41.8° and (c) 60°. State what happens to each ray, with a calculation for (a). (sin 30° = 0.5; the critical angle of the glass is 41.8°)

answer.model_answer_md: (a) $\sin e = 1.5 \times 0.5 = 0.75$, so the ray passes into air at about 48.6° from the normal, bending away from it (a little light is also reflected). (b) 41.8° is the critical angle: the refracted ray grazes along the surface (angle of refraction 90°). (c) 60° is more than the critical angle, so the ray is totally internally reflected back into the glass.

questions.solution_md: Refracted at 48.6°; grazes; TIR.

questions.stem_md: Pair each optical quantity in Column A with its typical value in Column B.

options.text_md: Refractive index of water
Refractive index of diamond
Critical angle of crown glass
Critical angle of diamond

questions.solution_md: Water → 1.33; diamond → 2.42; crown glass → about 42°; diamond → about 24°.

questions.stem_md: For each everyday sight in Column A, choose its cause from Column B.

options.text_md: A swimming pool looks shallower than it is
A thick mirror shows several images of a flame
A prism in a periscope turns light through 90°
The ray leaving a glass block is parallel to the incident ray

match_right.text_md: Repeated partial reflection inside the glass

questions.stem_md:
(a) Write down the laws that govern the bending of light at a boundary, and define the absolute refractive index of a medium. [3]

(b) Light of wavelength 5.0 × 10⁻⁷ m in air enters a flint glass of refractive index 1.6. Calculate (i) the speed of light in the glass, (ii) its wavelength in the glass, and (iii) its frequency. (c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s) [3]

(c) (i) Which of the three quantities in (b) is the same in air and in glass? Why? (ii) Does the colour of the light change in the glass? (iii) State two conditions under which a ray passes from one medium to another without bending. [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) (1) The incident ray, the refracted ray and the normal at the point of incidence lie in the same plane. (2) For a given pair of media and colour, sin i ÷ sin r is a constant (Snell’s law). Absolute refractive index: speed of light in vacuum ÷ speed of light in the medium.

(b) (i) $v = \dfrac{3.0 \times 10^{8}}{1.6} = 1.875 \times 10^{8}$ m/s. (ii) $\lambda = \dfrac{5.0 \times 10^{-7}}{1.6} \approx 3.1 \times 10^{-7}$ m. (iii) $f = \dfrac{3.0 \times 10^{8}}{5.0 \times 10^{-7}} = 6.0 \times 10^{14}$ Hz.

(c) (i) The frequency: it is set by the source. (ii) No: colour depends on frequency, which does not change. (iii) When the ray falls along the normal; when the two media have equal refractive indices.

questions.solution_md: Laws and definition; three calculations; frequency, colour and two conditions.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Describe, as you would draw it, the path of a ray of light falling obliquely on a rectangular glass block, marking the angle of incidence, the angle of refraction, the angle of emergence and the lateral displacement. [3]

(b) A ray strikes a glass block (refractive index 1.5) at an angle of incidence of 60°. (i) Find the sine of the angle of refraction, and the angle. (ii) State the angle of emergence. (sin 60° = 0.866) [3]

(c) (i) Name the factors on which lateral displacement depends. (ii) Explain how a thick plane mirror forms more than one image of a candle, and which image is the brightest. [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The ray bends towards the normal on entering the block (angle of refraction smaller than the angle of incidence) and away from the normal on leaving it at the opposite face. The emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray. The lateral displacement is the perpendicular distance between the incident ray produced (dotted) and the emergent ray; normals are drawn at both points.

(b) (i) $\sin r = \dfrac{0.866}{1.5} = 0.577$, so $r \approx 35.3^\circ$. (ii) $60^\circ$, the same as the angle of incidence, because the faces are parallel.

(c) (i) Thickness of the block, angle of incidence, refractive index (colour of light). (ii) Some light reflects from the front glass surface, giving a faint image; most enters the glass, reflects at the silvered back and comes out, giving the brightest image; repeated reflections inside the glass give further, fainter images.

questions.solution_md: Ray path; Snell’s law and e = i; factors and thick mirror.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Define real depth and apparent depth, and write the relation between them and the refractive index. [3]

(b) A pond is 2.0 m deep and the refractive index of water is 4/3. (i) How deep does the pond appear from directly above? (ii) By how much is its floor raised? (iii) A boy who is 1.5 m tall plans to wade across it because it looks shallow. Is this safe? [3]

(c) A vessel holds a liquid 20 cm deep, and a mark on its floor appears 15 cm below the surface. (i) Find the refractive index of the liquid. (ii) Explain why a pencil dipped slantwise into the liquid looks bent. (iii) How would the apparent depth change if the mark were viewed at a slant? [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Real depth: actual depth of an object below the surface. Apparent depth: the depth at which it appears when seen from the rarer medium. $\mu = \dfrac{\text{real depth}}{\text{apparent depth}}$ (for viewing from directly above).

(b) (i) $\dfrac{2.0}{4/3} = 1.5$ m. (ii) $2.0 - 1.5 = 0.5$ m. (iii) No: the real depth, 2.0 m, is more than his height.

(c) (i) $\mu = \dfrac{20}{15} = 1.33$. (ii) Each point of the immersed part appears raised (light bends away from the normal as it leaves the liquid), so the immersed part seems lifted and the pencil looks bent at the surface. (iii) It would appear even smaller: the mark looks still nearer the surface.

questions.solution_md: Definitions; pond; liquid.

questions.stem_md:
(a) What is meant by the critical angle? State the two conditions necessary for total internal reflection. [3]

(b) (i) Calculate the critical angle for a glass of refractive index 1.5. (ii) The critical angle of a certain liquid is 45°. Find its refractive index. (sin 45° = 0.7071) [3]

(c) (i) Describe, as you would draw it, how a right-angled isosceles prism turns a ray through 180°. (ii) Why is total reflection possible inside such a glass prism? (iii) Give two advantages of using such a prism instead of a plane mirror. [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The critical angle is the angle of incidence in the denser medium for which the angle of refraction in the rarer medium is 90°. Conditions: light travels from an optically denser to a rarer medium; the angle of incidence exceeds the critical angle.

(b) (i) $\sin C = \dfrac{1}{1.5} = 0.667$, so $C \approx 41.8^\circ$. (ii) $\mu = \dfrac{1}{0.7071} = 1.414$.

(c) (i) The ray enters the hypotenuse face along the normal (undeviated), meets one short face at 45°, is totally reflected to the other short face, meets it at 45°, is totally reflected again, and leaves the hypotenuse face along the normal, travelling back parallel to its original path. (ii) The angle of incidence, 45°, is greater than the critical angle of glass (about 42°). (iii) All the light is reflected, so the image is brighter; only one image is formed; there is no silvering to fade.

questions.solution_md: Definition and conditions; two calculations; 180° prism and advantages.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Describe, as you would draw it, the path of a ray of monochromatic light through a triangular glass prism, marking the angle of deviation. [3]

(b) A ray falls at 48° on one face of an equilateral glass prism (refractive index 1.5). (i) Find the angle of refraction at the first face. (ii) Find the angle of incidence at the second face. (iii) The ray emerges at 49.2°; find the angle of deviation. (sin 48° = 0.743) [3]

(c) (i) Name two factors other than the angle of incidence on which the deviation depends. (ii) In (b), the ray inside the prism is almost parallel to the base. What does this tell you about the deviation? (iii) Give one way in which a prism differs from a glass block in its effect on a ray. [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The ray bends towards the normal at the first face and away from the normal at the second face, so it is turned towards the base. The angle of deviation is the angle between the incident ray produced forward and the emergent ray produced backward.

(b) (i) $\sin r_{1} = \dfrac{0.743}{1.5} = 0.495$, so $r_{1} \approx 29.7^\circ$. (ii) $r_{2} = 60 - 29.7 = 30.3$, that is about $30.3^\circ$. (iii) $\delta = i + e - A = 48 + 49.2 - 60 = 37.2$, that is $37.2^\circ$.

(c) (i) The angle of the prism; the refractive index of the glass (also the colour of light). (ii) The ray passes symmetrically, so the deviation is (nearly) the minimum deviation. (iii) A glass block gives an emergent ray parallel to the incident ray; a prism deviates the ray towards its base.

questions.solution_md: Ray path; angles and deviation; factors.
